name: Handoffs
question: Who should own the conversation now?
summary: One agent transfers the live conversation to a specialist, who then answers the user directly. A supervisor keeps control; a handoff gives it away. Handoffs are exposed to the model as tools, such as transfer_to_card_agent in the OpenAI Agents SDK, so routing depends on their names and descriptions. What history travels with the handoff decides whether the user must repeat themselves.
useCases: Support bots with distinct specialist areas: cards, loans, fraud
Conversations whose owner should change midway
Specialists that need their own tools, permissions or instructions

items.detail: the triage model routes on them, so make them distinct

the specialist owns the rest of the turn

steps: Build specialists with narrow, non-overlapping responsibilities
Write handoff descriptions that say exactly when to transfer
Pass the facts the specialist needs as a typed payload, not the whole transcript
Cap turns, and allow hand-backs only with a limit on hops
pitfalls: Overlapping descriptions cause misroutes and ping-pong
Passing no context makes users repeat themselves
Peer-to-peer handoffs without caps can loop
remember: Distinct descriptions, typed payloads, capped hops.
caption: Illustrative: a 3-field payload replaces 14 messages of history, and the user no longer has to repeat details.

steps.title: Build specialists
steps.text: Three agents, each owning one area: cards, loans and fraud. Each has its own instructions and could have its own tools and permissions.

steps.title: Write distinct descriptions
steps.text: Handoffs reach the model as tools named transfer_to_card_agent and so on. The triage model routes on these descriptions, so they must not overlap.

steps.title: Attach them to triage
steps.text: handoffs=[...] gives triage one transfer tool per specialist. Triage only decides who owns the chat; it does not answer.

steps.title: Pass a typed payload
steps.text: input_type makes the model fill in a CardCase (last four digits and reason) when it hands off, and on_handoff stores it where the card agent’s instructions can read it.

steps.title: Trim the history
steps.text: input_filter removes earlier tool calls from what the card agent sees. It gets the conversation and the payload, not every intermediate step.

steps.title: Cap the turns
steps.text: max_turns bounds the whole run; going past it raises MaxTurnsExceeded. The card agent now owns the chat and resolves it in 2 turns.

Each specialist carries its own instructions, tools and permissions

playgroundGuide.scenario: Tarang Telecom’s triage agent hands 20 sample chats to recharge, porting and roaming specialists. A chat that reaches the right specialist with the details it needs takes 3 turns of about 1.5k tokens each. A user asked to repeat details adds 3 turns; each extra hop adds a turn.

Allow or forbid hand-backs to triage, and set max_turns.

presets.name: Overlapping, cold start
presets.expect: 60% overlap routes 14 of 20 correctly (70%). With hand-backs off, 6 chats are stuck; every user repeats their details. 14 resolved at 12.9k tokens each.

presets.name: Distinct descriptions
presets.expect: 10% overlap routes 19 of 20 (95%), but the specialist still starts cold, so all 20 users repeat themselves. 19 resolved at 9.5k tokens each.

presets.name: Full history
presets.expect: Passing all 14 messages ends the repeats (0), but adds 5.6k tokens to every handoff: 19 resolved at 10.6k each.

presets.name: Ping-pong
presets.expect: 80% overlap with hand-backs on: every chat is resolved, but misroutes bounce 4 times, so handoffs rise to 4.2 per chat; a summary still leaves 4 users repeating.

missions.hint: Make the descriptions distinct: 20% overlap or less.

missions.text: Get “asked to repeat” to 0 without passing the full history.
Allow hand-backs and keep handoffs per chat at 2 or fewer, with all 20 chats resolved.
missions.hint: Hand-backs rescue misroutes, but each misroute bounces more when descriptions overlap. Lower the overlap and leave enough turns.

practice.scenario: Tarang Telecom, a fictional operator, runs a support bot that first classifies each chat and then hands it to a recharge, porting or roaming specialist. Each handoff carries a small typed payload (mobile number, circle, issue) instead of the whole transcript, and each specialist has its own tools and permissions.

industries.use: Triage to recharge, porting and roaming specialists
Triage to card, loan and fraud agents with separate permissions

practice.analogy: A hospital reception desk. The receptionist asks two questions, writes a short referral slip and sends you to the right department, which takes over your case.

library.name: OpenAI Agents SDK
library.what: Agents list the specialists they can hand off to; each handoff is a tool the model can call, with optional typed input, history filters and a callback.

samples.code:
import asyncio
from pydantic import BaseModel
from agents import Agent, Runner, RunContextWrapper, handoff
from agents.extensions import handoff_filters

class PortRequest(BaseModel):
    mobile: str
    circle: str
    issue: str

async def log_port(ctx: RunContextWrapper[None], data: PortRequest):
    print("porting handoff:", data.mobile, data.circle)

recharge = Agent(name="Recharge agent",
                 handoff_description="Failed or missing prepaid recharges and plan changes.",
                 instructions="Resolve recharge issues. Never ask again for details you were given.")
porting = Agent(name="Porting agent",
                handoff_description="Moving a number to or from Tarang (MNP), UPC codes.",
                instructions="Resolve porting issues using the payload you receive.")

triage = Agent(
    name="Triage",
    instructions="Classify the problem and hand off. Do not answer it yourself.",
    handoffs=[recharge,
              handoff(porting, input_type=PortRequest, on_handoff=log_port,
                      input_filter=handoff_filters.remove_all_tools)],
)

async def main():
    result = await Runner.run(triage, "My UPC code expired before the port finished",
                              max_turns=8)
    print(result.last_agent.name, "->", result.final_output)

asyncio.run(main())

numericDrill.question: Without handoff payloads, 40% of 1,000 transferred chats make the user repeat details, adding 4 turns each. A typed payload removes the repeats. At 1.5k tokens per turn, how many tokens (in thousands) does the payload save across the 1,000 chats?
numericDrill.answer: Chats with repeats: 0.4 × 1,000 = 400. Extra turns: 400 × 4 = 1,600. Tokens: 1,600 × 1.5k = 2,400k tokens, or 2.4 million.

interview.question: When do you use a handoff rather than calling a specialist as a tool?
interview.answer: Use a handoff when the specialist should own the rest of the conversation and answer the user directly. Use agent-as-tool when a manager should keep control, call the specialist for a sub-answer and compose the reply itself.

interview.question: Why do handoff descriptions matter so much?
interview.answer: Handoffs are exposed to the model as tools, so the triage model chooses among them from their names and descriptions. Overlapping descriptions leave it guessing, which causes misroutes and back-and-forth transfers.

mistakes.mistake: Don’t pass the whole transcript on every handoff.
mistakes.fix: Pass a small typed payload and filter the history.
Cap turns and hops so two specialists cannot ping-pong.

quiz.question: A bank’s triage agent keeps sending EMI questions to the card agent. The card and loan handoffs have almost identical descriptions. What is the fix?
options: Distinct descriptions that say exactly when to transfer to each specialist
Passing the full history on every handoff
quiz.explanation: Handoffs are tools, and the model routes on their descriptions. Overlapping descriptions leave it guessing.

quiz.question: In the OpenAI Agents SDK, what is the default tool name for a handoff to an agent named “Refund agent”?
quiz.explanation: Handoffs appear to the model as tools named transfer_to_<agent_name> by default.

quiz.question: When should a telecom support bot use a handoff rather than calling a specialist as a tool? Select all that apply.
options: The specialist should talk to the user directly for the rest of the chat
The specialist has its own permissions and should own the case
A manager must combine three specialists’ answers into one reply
The manager needs a one-off sub-answer inside its own reply
quiz.explanation: A handoff transfers ownership. When one agent should keep control and compose the reply, call specialists as tools.

quiz.question: Of 2,000 transferred chats, 30% make the user repeat their details, adding 3 turns each at about 1.2k tokens a turn. How many tokens do the repeats cost?
quiz.explanation: 0.3 × 2,000 = 600 chats × 3 turns × 1.2k = 2,160k tokens, about 2.16 million.

quiz.question: An airline’s rebooking and baggage agents hand a chat back and forth until the run passes max_turns. What does the OpenAI Agents SDK do?
options: Hands the chat to a human automatically
quiz.explanation: Exceeding max_turns raises MaxTurnsExceeded, which you can catch to escalate.

quiz.question: What is input_filter for on a handoff?
options: Choosing which agent receives the handoff
Controlling which parts of the conversation history the receiving agent sees
quiz.explanation: An input filter transforms the history passed on, for example removing earlier tool calls.

quiz.question: An insurer’s claims bot bounces chats between its policy and claims agents. What can cause this? Select all that apply.
options: A typed payload on each handoff
quiz.explanation: Ping-pong comes from ambiguous ownership and missing limits. A typed payload helps the receiver; it does not cause bouncing.

quiz.question: In LangGraph, what does a handoff tool return to move control to another agent in the parent graph?
options: A plain string naming the agent
quiz.explanation: LangGraph handoff tools return a Command that names the next node, updates state and targets the parent graph.

quiz.question: A bank’s triage routes 500 chats with 88% accuracy. Each misroute costs 2 extra handoffs before the chat lands. How many extra handoffs is that?
quiz.explanation: 12% of 500 = 60 misroutes × 2 = 120 extra handoffs.

quiz.question: An airline wants the triage model to supply the PNR and the reason when it hands off to the refunds agent. Which feature fits?
quiz.explanation: input_type makes the model fill in a structured payload when it calls the handoff.

quiz.question: A hospital’s intake agent hands patients to a scheduling agent. What should travel with the handoff? Select all that apply.
options: A typed payload with the facts scheduling needs
The conversation with earlier tool calls filtered out
Every internal tool call and raw tool output
Nothing, so the specialist starts unbiased
quiz.explanation: Pass the needed facts and a trimmed history. Raw tool output wastes tokens; nothing at all makes the patient repeat themselves.

quiz.question: A travel assistant built with langgraph-swarm resumes a returning user’s chat. Which agent answers first?
options: The agent recorded in the active_agent state key
The agent with the shortest description
quiz.explanation: langgraph-swarm tracks active_agent so a conversation resumes with whichever agent last owned it.

quiz.question: A student-support triage agent hands a fee query to the fees agent. Who replies to the student next?
options: The triage agent, relaying the fees agent’s answer
Both agents, one after the other
No one until a human approves
quiz.explanation: After a handoff the specialist becomes the active agent and answers directly.

quiz.question: How does a handoff differ from model routing?
options: Routing picks a model for one request; a handoff moves ownership of the conversation, with its state, to another agent
A handoff always uses a smaller model
Routing needs several agents; handoffs need one
quiz.explanation: Routing is a per-request model choice. A handoff changes which agent owns the rest of the conversation.

quiz.question: Passing the full history adds 14 messages of about 0.4k tokens to each handoff, and chats average 1.4 handoffs. How many extra tokens per chat is that?
quiz.explanation: 14 × 0.4k = 5.6k per handoff; 5.6k × 1.4 = 7.84k per chat.

quiz.question: What is the on_handoff callback useful for? Select all that apply.
options: Logging or fetching data at the moment of the handoff
Storing the typed payload where the specialist can read it
Choosing which agent the handoff goes to
quiz.explanation: on_handoff runs when the handoff happens, so it can log, fetch data or store the payload. The model chooses the target; max_turns is a run setting.

quiz.question: An AutoGen support team must pause when an agent needs the customer to supply an OTP. Which termination condition fits?
quiz.explanation: HandoffTermination stops the team when an agent hands off to the named target, here the user.

quiz.question: The fraud agent can freeze cards; the triage agent cannot. Why keep permissions per specialist?
options: Each agent gets only the privileges its job needs, so a misrouted or manipulated agent can do less harm
quiz.explanation: Per-agent permissions apply least privilege: the tools that can change things sit only with the agent that owns that job.

quiz.question: Which make good handoff descriptions for a telecom bot’s specialists? Select all that apply.
options: Naming topics that are distinct for each specialist
Using one generic sentence for all of them, for consistency
quiz.explanation: Specific, distinct, non-overlapping descriptions give the triage model something to route on. A shared generic sentence removes that.

quiz.question: On 20 test chats, triage routes 17 correctly. How many more must it get right to reach the 90% target?
quiz.explanation: 90% of 20 is 18, so it needs one more correct route.
